purpose: How does collecting more independent readings per jig change the chance of detecting a declared mean shift?
meaning: Declare a positive-direction mean shift and a known common reading spread before collecting data. Independent readings per group determine the standard error of the mean difference; a fixed one-sided cutoff then separates rejection from non-rejection under the assumed shift.

definition.setting: A workshop plans a comparison of current and proposed calibration jigs. It will collect n independent cutting-error readings from each jig. Before collection, enter an assumed true increase δ in mean error and a known common reading standard deviation σ. Follow n into the standard error, then read the null and assumed-shift exceedance curves at the same rejection cutoff c. A positive increase is a direction to detect, not automatically an improvement.

signature.n: Whole number of independent readings per group
signature.N: Total number of readings across the two equal groups
signature.δ: Assumed true increase in population mean error, in millimetres
signature.σ: Known common reading standard deviation, in millimetres
signature.SE: Standard error of the two-group mean difference, in millimetres
signature.c: Predeclared positive-direction rejection cutoff, in millimetres
signature.α: Maximum null rejection probability, fixed at 0.05
signature.β: Non-rejection probability at the entered true difference
signature.1−β: Rejection probability at the entered true difference

conditions: The two groups are independent; readings within each group are independent and normally distributed, with known common positive standard deviation σ. The predeclared one-sided test rejects when the future mean difference exceeds c, testing a nonpositive true difference against a positive one at significance level α=0.05. The assumed effect δ is a planning input rather than an estimate from observed data. Use whole n from 2 to 64 readings per group, δ from 0 to 2 mm and σ from 0.25 to 2 mm. There are 2n readings in total. At δ=0 the rejection probability is α and the complement β is null non-rejection; β is a Type II error probability only when δ>0. Normal tails and the critical quantile are numerical approximations. No observations, random allocations, empirical power estimate or causal guarantee are generated. Estimated rather than known spread, unequal groups, paired readings and two-sided testing require different procedures.

properties.derivation: Each group mean has variance σ²/n. Independence makes the mean-difference variance add to 2σ²/n, giving the stated standard error. Under a true difference δ, the standardized mean difference is normal. The standard normal CDF Φ converts a standardized cutoff into a cumulative probability. The upper-tail rejection probability above c equals Φ((δ−c)/SE) by normal symmetry. Replication reduces standard error by a square-root factor, while changing δ changes the planning alternative. Type II error refers to non-rejection only for a positive alternative; a failure to reject never proves the null.

applications.limitations: The two groups are independent; readings within each group are independent and normally distributed, with known common positive standard deviation σ. The predeclared one-sided test rejects when the future mean difference exceeds c, testing a nonpositive true difference against a positive one at significance level α=0.05. The assumed effect δ is a planning input rather than an estimate from observed data. Use whole n from 2 to 64 readings per group, δ from 0 to 2 mm and σ from 0.25 to 2 mm. There are 2n readings in total. At δ=0 the rejection probability is α and the complement β is null non-rejection; β is a Type II error probability only when δ>0. Normal tails and the critical quantile are numerical approximations. No observations, random allocations, empirical power estimate or causal guarantee are generated. Estimated rather than known spread, unequal groups, paired readings and two-sided testing require different procedures.
